title: Timers: an off-delay light and an on-delay filter
summary: Use a TOF timer to keep a light on after a button is released, and a TON timer to ignore a sensor blip that is too short.
scope: Passing means your program behaved correctly in the simulator on this computer. It says nothing about a real machine, its timing or its safety, and it does not show how a real button bounces or how fast a real sensor answers.
objectives: Keep an output on for a fixed time after its input drops, with a timer instance called on every scan.
Ignore an input that is on for less than a fixed time, and say which of the two delays belongs to the start of a signal and which to its end.

stages.title: Objective
stages.body: In src/Delays.st two timers are declared, HoldTimer (TOF) and FilterTimer (TON), and the program copies Button to Light and Sensor to Confirmed. Make Light stay ON for {{t:300}} ms after Button is released, and make Confirmed turn ON only after Sensor has stayed ON for {{t:200}} ms.
stages.checkpoint: You can say which of the two timers keeps an output on after its input falls, and which one waits before it turns its output on.

stages.title: Predict
stages.body: The scenario presses Button at {{t:100}} ms and releases it at {{t:300}} ms. Sensor blips ON from {{t:100}} ms to {{t:140}} ms and is ON again from {{t:500}} ms to {{t:900}} ms. Predict Light and Confirmed at {{t:200}}, {{t:450}}, {{t:650}}, and {{t:800}} ms.
stages.checkpoint: {{v:Delays.Light=true,Delays.Confirmed=false@200|Light ON, Confirmed OFF}} at {{t:200}} ms; {{v:Delays.Light=true,Delays.Confirmed=false@450|Light ON, Confirmed OFF}} at {{t:450}} ms; {{v:Delays.Light=false,Delays.Confirmed=false@650|both OFF}} at {{t:650}} ms; {{v:Delays.Light=false,Delays.Confirmed=true@800|Confirmed ON, Light OFF}} at {{t:800}} ms.

stages.title: Edit
stages.body: Correct the starting program, save it, then press {{ui:learn.check}}. The starting program copies the inputs to the outputs, so Light is already OFF at {{t:450}} ms and Confirmed turns ON with the short blip at {{t:100}} ms. Change it so that Light stays ON until {{t:300}} ms after Button is released, and Confirmed turns ON only when Sensor has been ON for {{t:200}} ms without a break. Write the statements yourself: the declarations are already there.
stages.checkpoint: {{ui:learn.check}} reports the scenario of this lesson as passed.

stages.title: Run
stages.body: Press {{ui:learn.check}}. ZPLC runs your saved program against the scenario of this lesson and lists every assertion that failed.
stages.checkpoint: The scenario is named Delays and contains {{assertions}} assertions.

stages.title: Observe
stages.body: Follow Light and Confirmed in the trace: the short blip never turns Confirmed ON, Light is still ON at {{t:450}} ms although Button went OFF at {{t:300}} ms, and Confirmed rises about {{t:200}} ms after Sensor came back at {{t:500}} ms.
stages.checkpoint: Light falls about {{t:300}} ms after Button, and Confirmed rises about {{t:200}} ms after the second Sensor pulse.

stages.title: Reflect
stages.body: Once it passes, swap the roles in your head: what would each output do if its delay sat at the other end of its input? Then imagine your timer calls running only while Button is TRUE: what would Confirmed do?
stages.checkpoint: TON delays the start and TOF delays the end; each answers a different question about a signal. A timer that is not called keeps its clock and its Q as they were, so Light would never fall and Confirmed would never rise.

hints.text: Look at the two copy statements: nothing stands between each input and its output. For each output, ask whether its delay belongs to the start of its input or to the end of it.
Write HoldTimer(IN := Button, PT := T#300ms); Light := HoldTimer.Q; FilterTimer(IN := Sensor, PT := T#200ms); Confirmed := FilterTimer.Q;

faultCases: The starting program copies the inputs to the outputs, so Light is already OFF at {{t:450}} ms and Confirmed turns ON with the short blip at {{t:100}} ms.
